title: Regimes: the two questions that organise everything
hook:
Imagine you have been away for six months with no phone and no news. You land at the airport and someone hands you exactly two facts about the Indian economy: whether growth is speeding up or slowing down, and whether inflation is rising or falling. Nothing else. No oil price, no RBI statement, no election results.

Surprisingly, you could make a decent guess at a lot from those two facts alone: what the RBI is probably doing, whether bond yields are likely rising, which sectors have been leading the market and which have been left behind. Those two directions together define what investors call a regime, and the regime is the frame that holds every other chapter in this explainer together.

This chapter builds the frame. It explains the four regimes, shows where India sits today, and then looks at what our own data says about how sectors behaved in each one. That last part comes with an honest warning, and the warning is the most important thing in the chapter.
short: Two questions name the regime: is growth accelerating or slowing, and is inflation rising or falling? The answers give four regimes: goldilocks, reflation, stagflation and deflation.
Regimes are about direction, not level. Inflation can be low and still be in a rising regime.
India is in reflation on the latest published data, and market prices agree. But this reflation is supply-led, driven by oil, which makes it worse for oil users than the textbook kind.
In our data, realty, metals and PSU banks beat the Nifty after reflation readings, while gold and pharma lagged. None of it clears a fair statistical bar, so treat it as a prior, not a signal.
The most likely next regime is stagflation: inflation still climbing on fuel while higher rates slow activity.

sections.heading: Two questions, four answers
sections.html:
The idea is simple enough to draw on a napkin. Draw a horizontal line for growth: to the right, growth is speeding up; to the left, it is slowing down. Draw a vertical line for inflation: up means inflation is rising, down means it is falling. You now have four boxes, and every month the economy sits in one of them.

  • Goldilocks: growth up, inflation down. Not too hot, not too cold. Companies sell more while their costs stay tame, and the central bank has room to cut rates. The friendliest box for stocks.
  • Reflation: growth up, inflation up. The economy is running hot. Sales are rising, but so are prices and, before long, interest rates. Good for companies that sell commodities or build things, less good for those whose costs are rising.
  • Stagflation: growth down, inflation up. The worst of both worlds. Demand weakens while costs keep climbing, and the central bank cannot help because cutting rates would make inflation worse. The hardest box for equities.
  • Deflation: growth down, inflation down. A slowdown with falling prices. The central bank cuts, bonds rally, and investors hide in steady businesses that sell things people buy in any year.

Here's the subtle bit that trips people up. These boxes are about direction, not level. India can have low inflation and still be in a rising-inflation regime, if inflation was even lower three months ago. Growth can be strong and still be in a slowing regime, if it was stronger before. Markets care about change because prices already reflect the level. What surprises investors, and moves stocks, is the turn.

To place India on the map, we use two official series. For growth, the index of industrial production, or IIP, which tracks factory, mining and electricity output every month. For inflation, the consumer price index, or CPI. We compare each with where it stood three months earlier: up or down. That gives the box.

sections.heading: Where India sits today, and the trail that got it there
sections.html:
Now the map with real data on it.

[[fig:1]]

The quadrant on the left plots India month by month since early 2026. The horizontal position is the change in industrial growth over three months; the vertical position is the change in inflation. The large dot is the latest reading, and the small dots trace the path that led there. Read the trail from oldest to newest. In the spring, India sat in the stagflation box: inflation was already rising as oil climbed, while industrial growth was slowing. Then, through the summer, growth picked up while inflation kept rising, and the dots crossed into reflation. The panel on the right states the latest reading in words.

Notice that the dots barely move up and down but swing a lot left and right. That is typical. Inflation moves slowly and steadily; industrial production is noisy and jumps around month to month. So a single month's move across the vertical line deserves less weight than a sustained drift.

The caption also flags a gap. The statistics office rebased the CPI, changing the basket of goods and the reference year, and that leaves a hole in our trail in 2025. It is a reminder that the official data has seams.

Which is why we cross-check with markets. The panel also reports a market-implied regime, built from two prices. Copper against gold: copper is an industrial metal that rises when the world is building, gold is a refuge that rises when investors are nervous, so copper beating gold says markets expect growth. And Brent crude, year on year, as a quick read on inflation pressure. Right now both say reflation. When the official data and market prices agree, the label is more trustworthy. When they disagree, markets are often early.

sections.heading: Why this reflation is not the textbook kind
sections.html:
The textbook reflation is demand-led. Consumers and companies are spending more, factories are busy, and prices rise because demand is outrunning supply. In that world, rising inflation is a symptom of health. Most companies can pass on higher costs because their customers are flush.

This reflation is different. It is supply-led. Inflation is rising mainly because oil got scarce and expensive after the war in the Gulf, not because Indians are spending more. A supply-led rise in prices is closer to a tax than a boom: money that would have gone on other things now goes on fuel, much of it to foreign oil producers.

That distinction matters a great deal for which sectors win. In a demand-led reflation, almost every cyclical sector does well. In a supply-led one, there is a clear split. Companies that sell energy or commodities collect the windfall. Companies that burn energy or buy commodities, such as airlines, paint makers, tyre makers and consumer goods companies whose packaging and raw materials are oil-based, see their margins squeezed. The same box on the map hides two very different economies.

A supply-led reflation is a tax dressed up as a boom. The regime label is the same; the winners are not.

It also changes what comes next. A demand-led reflation usually ends with the central bank gently cooling things down. A supply-led one has a nastier exit. Inflation keeps climbing as fuel costs pass through to transport, food and everything else, while the RBI raises rates to defend the rupee and contain prices. Higher rates then slow activity. Growth turns down while inflation is still rising, and the dot slides left, into stagflation.

That is why the most likely next regime is stagflation. The global inputs, high US bond yields and expensive oil, and the Indian ones, a hiking RBI and a fiscal squeeze from subsidies, all point the same way.

sections.heading: What our data says sectors did after a reflation reading
sections.html:
Theory says reflation should favour commodity producers and builders and punish defensives. What does India's own record say? We took every month since 2016 that the data placed in reflation and measured how each sector did against the Nifty over the following month.

[[fig:2]]

Read the chart from top to bottom. Bars to the right are sectors that beat the Nifty in the month after a reflation reading; bars to the left lagged it. The number next to each bar includes a t-statistic, which we will come back to.

At the top sits realty. That fits the story: when growth is picking up and inflation is rising, property looks like a real asset that holds value, demand for homes and offices rises, and developers are highly geared to the cycle. Next come metals and PSU banks. Metal companies sell the very commodities whose prices are rising. State-owned banks tend to be the most cyclical part of the banking sector, with large exposure to industry and infrastructure, so a growth pickup helps their loan books most. Energy and private banks are mildly positive.

At the bottom are the defensives. Pharma sells medicines people need regardless of the cycle, so when the cycle heats up investors rotate away from it. Gold lags most of all: when growth is accelerating, the appetite for a safe haven fades and money moves into risk. FMCG and autos sit slightly negative, which fits the cost-squeeze logic: their raw material bills rise with inflation, and they cannot always pass it on quickly.

All of this makes intuitive sense. And that is exactly the moment to be careful.

sections.heading: The honest caveat: why none of this is a signal
sections.html:
Here's the uncomfortable truth behind the chart. We did not test one idea. We tested four regimes across twelve sectors, which is forty-eight separate comparisons. And when you run that many tests, some will look impressive purely by chance.

Think of it with a coin. Toss a fair coin ten times and getting eight or more heads is unusual. But hand a coin to a hundred people, ask each to toss it ten times, and someone will almost certainly do it. That person has not found a magic coin. You just ran enough trials for luck to produce a winner.

The t-statistic measures how far a result is from zero relative to how noisy it is. For a single test, the conventional bar for calling something real is a t-statistic of about two. But with forty-eight tests, you would expect two or three cells to clear that bar by luck alone. So the bar has to rise. A fair bar for forty-eight tests, adjusting for the number of tries, is noticeably higher, as the caption shows.

And the result? The strongest of all forty-eight cells, gold's lag in reflation, falls short of that fair bar. So does realty at the top. Not one regime-by-sector result in our data clears it.

Every bar in the chart tells a plausible story. Not one of them clears the bar that proves it.

That does not mean the patterns are false. They line up with economic logic and with what has been observed in other markets. It means our sample, roughly a decade of Indian monthly data, is too short and too noisy to prove them. So we treat them as priors: reasonable starting assumptions to lean on lightly, not signals to trade on. None of these regime tilts is in the stock-picking model.

One more honesty note. The regime labels on the history cards below are qualitative summaries of each period, based on what is well documented about growth and inflation at the time, not computed by the quadrant. The bar chart above is computed. Keep the two separate in your head.

sections.heading: How to use a regime map without fooling yourself
sections.html:
A regime map is a frame, not a forecast. Used well, it stops you from fighting the tide. Used badly, it becomes a reason to overtrade. A few rules help.

  • Mind the lag. IIP is published several weeks after the month it describes, and it gets revised. By the time the data confirms a regime, markets have often moved. That is why the market-implied regime is a useful early warning.
  • Transitions matter more than labels. The biggest market moves tend to happen when the economy crosses a line, especially from reflation into stagflation. Spending time in a box is less important than spotting the exit.
  • Size it as a tilt, not a bet. Since none of the sector patterns clears a fair bar, a regime should nudge how much you hold in a sector, not decide whether you hold it at all.
  • Ask what kind of regime it is. Supply-led or demand-led changes the winners, as this cycle shows.

Used this way, the regime is the connective tissue of the whole explainer. The RBI chapter tells you how rates respond. The oil and dollar chapters tell you where the inflation comes from. The drawdowns chapter tells you how deep falls get. The regime tells you which of those forces is in charge right now.

history.title: Deflation: the commodity collapse
history.story:
China was slowing, its currency was devalued, and the world's commodity boom finally broke. Oil slid to its lowest in more than a decade early in 2016, and steel prices collapsed as cheap Chinese steel flooded the world. Indian steelmakers were in such trouble that in February 2016 the government imposed a minimum price on many steel imports to keep them alive.

Inflation was falling, and RBI Governor Raghuram Rajan cut rates through 2015. Growth worries dominated. It was a market for bonds, which rallied as yields fell, and for steady defensive businesses like consumer staples and pharma.
history.lesson: In deflation, bonds and defensives lead, and the companies that sell commodities suffer most.

history.title: Goldilocks: the year everything worked
history.story:
In June 2017, CPI inflation fell to the lowest reading since the series began, led by falling food prices. Chief Economic Adviser Arvind Subramanian described it as a paradigm shift to low inflation. The messy GST switch was behind the economy by the autumn, growth was recovering, and monthly mutual fund investments were pouring in from households.

The result was a broad rally, and small caps led it by a wide margin as investors chased growth stories. It felt as though stocks could only go up.
history.lesson: Goldilocks lifts almost everything, and small caps most of all, which is exactly why the end of it hurts them most.

history.title: Stagflation: the hangover
history.story:
Oil climbed through the year and the rupee slid to record lows, pushing inflation up. In June 2018, the RBI under Urjit Patel raised rates for the first time in more than four years, and hiked again in August. Then came the IL&FS default, which froze credit for non-bank lenders and the small businesses that depended on them.

Rising costs met slowing activity. The small caps that had soared in 2017 fell hardest, many losing much of what they had gained.
history.lesson: Stagflation punishes the most speculative corner of the market first, and a credit freeze makes it worse.

history.title: Reflation: the reopening boom
history.story:
As economies reopened after the pandemic lockdowns, demand came roaring back while supply chains were still broken. Commodity prices surged. Steelmakers like Tata Steel posted record profits, and metal stocks became market darlings. At the Fed, Jerome Powell described the rise in inflation as transitory, and central banks kept money cheap.

Metals, energy and cyclical sectors led. It was the textbook, demand-led reflation: sales and prices rising together.
history.lesson: In a demand-led reflation, the companies selling commodities and capacity win, and almost every cyclical rides along.

history.title: Stagflation again: war and hikes
history.story:
Russia's invasion of Ukraine sent oil, wheat and fertiliser prices soaring. Inflation in India rose well above the RBI's comfort zone, and in May Governor Shaktikanta Das surprised the market with an unscheduled hike, followed by a string more. The Fed hiked at its fastest pace in decades.

Energy companies and banks held up, the latter helped by loan rates that reset upward. Technology stocks were hammered, with the IT index losing more than a quarter of its value over the year as higher US rates crushed the valuations of growth companies.
history.lesson: When stagflation is driven by rates, long-duration growth stocks fall hardest, while energy and banks hold up.

history.title: Reflation, turning
history.story:
The Iran war and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz sent oil sharply higher. Inflation rose with fuel, while industrial growth held up through the summer, so the data placed India in reflation. In October the RBI raised rates and tightened currency rules to defend the rupee.

But this is a supply-led reflation, closer to an oil tax than a boom, and the pressure is building towards the exit. Higher rates and costlier fuel are the classic recipe for growth to turn down while inflation is still rising.
history.lesson: The label says reflation; the risk is the turn to stagflation, and that turn is what to watch.

today:
On the latest published data, India's regime is [[val:regime]], with figures running to [[val:regime_month]]. Inflation is at [[val:cpi]], up [[val:cpi_3m]] over three months, and Brent sits at [[val:brent]] a barrel, so the inflation side is firmly rising. The growth side is the one to watch: it carried India into reflation over the summer, and it is the side that would carry it out.

Two releases decide the next move on the map: the September IIP and the October CPI. If industrial growth fades while inflation keeps climbing, the dot slides left into stagflation, and the sector picture changes with it.
sowhat:
While the regime holds, the data and the logic lean the same way, but only gently.

  • Lean towards commodity and capex exposure, such as metals, energy, infrastructure and PSU banks, over defensives and gold, sized as a weak prior rather than a conviction.
  • Be careful with companies whose costs are oil-linked, such as airlines, paints, tyres and some consumer goods. In a supply-led reflation they are on the wrong side of the windfall.
  • Remember the caveat: no regime-by-sector pattern in our data clears a fair statistical bar, and none is in the model. Tilt, don't bet.

What would flip it: growth turning down in the next IIP releases while CPI keeps rising. That is the move into stagflation, where the playbook shifts towards cash-rich, low-debt businesses, energy producers and genuine defensives, and away from rate-sensitive and speculative small caps.
